newsitem.title: USA: Sun-Diamond convicted over gifts to ex-USDA chief.
newsitem.headline: Sun-Diamond convicted over gifts to ex-USDA chief.

text.p: Sun-Diamond Growers of California, the nation's largest fruit cooperative, was convicted on Tuesday on all but one count of illegally giving gifts and favors to then Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy.
The agricultural firm was also convicted of taking part in a scheme to funnel illegal campaign contributions to Espy's brother Henry and of two charges of wire fraud.

The convictions -- the first to come out of the government's two-year investigation of the former Clinton cabinet member -- could have serious implications for pending cases in the probe and do not bode well for Espy and others still under investigation, legal experts said.

"Today's verdict reflects that juries are tired of what they regard as corruption in big business and government and it will give steam to the prosecutor's efforts to proceed further against other people in this matter," University of Georgetown law professor Paul Rothstein said.

"This gives our investigation some impetus," Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz, who is heading the widespread probe, told reporters after the verdict was announced. "Each case will be judged on its own merit ... but this should send a strong signal," he said.

Sun-Diamond said it was considering an immediate appeal of the conviction. "Sun-Diamond has consistently maintained that its conduct and relationship with the former Secretary of Agriculture has been lawful and proper," it said.
Espy lawyer Reid Weingarten said his client was not feeling any more pressure as a result of the verdict.
"I know that Mike Espy never provided any favors for Sun-Diamond ... I have complete confidence that at the end of the day, Mike Espy will be completely exonerated," he said.

Sun-Diamond, whose affiliates include Sun Maid raisins, Sunsweet prunes and Diamond Walnut, had been charged with violating nine criminal counts involving illegal gratuities and illegal campaign contributions to Espy and his brother in 1993 and 1994 while Espy headed the huge agriculture agency.
He resigned as a cabinet secretary in 1994 amid accusations that he had taken illegal gifts and favors from companies his agency was charged to regulate.

After deliberating for 9-1/2 hours over two days a jury found Sun-Diamond not guilty of only one of the counts, which alleged that the cooperative had paid transportation costs for Espy's girlfriend to accompany him to a conference in Greece.

The government said the company, acting through its Washington lobbyist Richard Douglas, a close personal friend of Espy, used the enticements of expensive gifts and favors to Espy and his girlfriend and campaign contributions to Henry Espy to try to sway Espy on important issues.

Sun-Diamond attorney Richard Hibey said the company was innocent of any wrongdoing and that the gifts, which included lavish meals, a luggage set and a weekend outing to the U.S. Tennis Open tournament in 1993, reflected the close friendship between Douglas and Espy, and nothing more.
Legal sources said the verdict was an important victory for prosectors, who had been accused of over-reaching their authority and of investigating relatively insignificant discretions.
"This is a very substantial victory for the independent counsel," said former U.S. prosecutor Joseph di Genova. "This obviously gives validation to his efforts.

So far the investigation has yielded five sets of criminal indictments and charges against more than a dozen individuals and concerns including the Washington lobbyist for Tyson Foods, the huge Arkansas-based chicken processor whose chairman has long had close ties with President Bill Clinton, a former governor of Arkansas.

Tyson Foods has been a focus of the Espy investigation since the start after it was learned the firm gave Espy and his girlfriend tickets to Super Bowl playoffs in 1993 and a scholarship potentially worth almost $10,000 to the girlfriend.
